mappings.note: Field pattern inside a current-carrying solenoid; LO-4 names the solenoid. Not LO-6: nothing is drawn and no line spacing is read, the answer is the field the current makes.
Uniformity of a long solenoid's internal field. LO-4, not LO-6, because the claim is about the field's value along the axis, not about a diagram.
All four options are field-line properties (closed curves, no intersection, tangent gives direction, N-to-S outside). LO-6 owns field-line interpretation; no current appears, so LO-4 is out.
Shape of a straight current-carrying wire's field - the first object LO-4 names. Not LO-5: no handedness rule is needed, only the pattern.
B proportional to I and inversely to r for a straight conductor - the quantitative half of 'describes the magnetic field produced by a straight conductor'.
Field line through the centre of a current loop is straight; LO-4 names the loop. Not LO-6, whose drawing objects are the bar magnet and the solenoid.
Soft-iron core strengthens the solenoid's field. The frame has no electromagnet outcome, so LO-4's solenoid is the correct home.
Factors setting the magnitude of the force on a current-carrying conductor. The field is the input here, not the output - that is what separates LO-1 from LO-4.
The false option is 'parallel equidistant lines represent zero field'; that is spacing-versus-strength, LO-6's second clause.
Opening the key removes the current, so LO-4's concentric circles vanish; what is left is the earth's uniform field drawn as parallel lines, an LO-6 spacing reading. Needs both.
A current loop's faces acquire polarity (LO-4), identified from the sense of the field lines (LO-6). Not LO-5 - the field direction is given, so no right-hand rule is applied.
The false statement is that a solenoid's pattern differs from a bar magnet's - LO-6 pairs exactly those two objects, so it leads; LO-4 second for the solenoid's own field.
Asks for the direction of the force on an electron and a proton, i.e. Fleming's left-hand rule (LO-5) acting through the LO-1 force. A direction is the graded answer, so LO-5 leads.
The only motor question in the chapter - what commercial motors use to rotate the armature. LO-1 is the motor outcome.
Two coils on one rod, momentary and oppositely directed kicks on make and break: mutual induction. LO-2, not LO-1, because a changing flux makes a current rather than a field pushing a conductor.
Answer is obtained by applying the right-hand thumb rule to a wire carrying current east to west. LO-5, not LO-4, because the graded output is a direction.
Uniform field inside a long solenoid; near-duplicate of item 2 and mapped the same way.
Assertion and reason are both about why a current-carrying conductor feels a force in a field - LO-1's mechanism, stated as field-on-field interaction.
The fuse as the protection against short circuit and overload - LO-7 names the fuse.
Whether a current-carrying rod's field exists inside as well as outside it - the spatial description of a straight conductor's field, LO-4.
Matching acceleration, velocity, speed and kinetic energy for a charge in a field; turns on the magnetic force doing no work. LO-1; no rule is applied, so not LO-5.
F = qvB sin(theta) - the magnitude of the magnetic force and when it peaks. Magnitude, not direction, so LO-1 rather than LO-5.
Superposing the fields of two current configurations at P (LO-4), with each contribution's into/out-of-page sense fixed by the right-hand rule (LO-5).
A net-neutral wire still feels a force because the charges inside it move - LO-1's mechanism exactly.
Whether the solenoid's field depends on its length and cross-section, and whether it is uniform inside - LO-4's description of the solenoid's field.
